title: Modi at IIT Kharagpur's 75th Year: 'Break the Limits, Unlock the Possibilities'
excerpt: At the platinum jubilee of India's first IIT, the Prime Minister interacted with 75 students, unveiled a commemorative coin, and pointed to poverty numbers, chip exports and Skyroot's rocket as proof that 'too late' is a mindset.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed the platinum jubilee celebrations of IIT Kharagpur on Saturday, November 21, marking 75 years of India's first Indian Institute of Technology, founded in 1951.
  • He interacted with 75 students under the '75 Voices for Viksit Bharat' initiative, viewed an exhibition of student innovation projects, and unveiled a commemorative coin for the institute's 75th year.
  • Modi told students the next two decades would be crucial to the 'Viksit Bharat' goal, urging a "nation first" mindset and citing semiconductors and the opened-up space sector as fields where India had acted after being told it was too late.
  • For diaspora alumni: the visit was Modi's first to the institute, and he singled out IIT Kharagpur alumnus Pawan Kumar Chandana, co-founder of Skyroot Aerospace, builder of India's first privately developed rocket.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday told the students of IIT Kharagpur that India had spent the last 12 years proving that limits are a mindset. Addressing the institute's platinum jubilee celebrations — 75 years since the founding of India's first Indian Institute of Technology in 1951 — Modi said the country had declared "loud and clear" its resolve to "break the limits and unlock the possibilities," and that the next two decades would be crucial to realising the 'Viksit Bharat' vision, The Hindu BusinessLine reported.

"Our strength is determined by how courageously we dare to challenge challenges. People often ask me about challenges. I tell them that it is in my very nature that I cannot rest without challenging a challenge."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister, at IIT Kharagpur

The visit

The Prime Minister arrived at around 9:45 a.m., in line with the schedule the Press Information Bureau had published: participation in the platinum jubilee celebrations, an address to the gathering, and an interaction with 75 students symbolising the institute's 75-year journey. At the event, held under the '75 Voices for Viksit Bharat' initiative, Modi engaged with selected students on India's path to becoming a developed nation, toured an exhibition of innovation projects and research prototypes — including work in agriculture, robotics, aerospace, drones and medicine — accompanied by institute director Professor Suman Chakraborty, and unveiled a commemorative silver coin marking 75 years of IIT Kharagpur, Careers360 reported. It was his first visit to the institute. From Kharagpur he was scheduled to travel to Bihar for development projects in Vaishali, and then to Lucknow for the 5th Kaushal Deekshant Samaroh at 5:30 p.m.

The argument: poverty, chips and rockets

Modi built the speech around three examples. On poverty, he said it had been treated for decades as a permanent problem — slogans were raised, but policy action stalled on the belief that a country of India's size could not eliminate it — and he cited a World Bank report in claiming around 50 crore people had been brought out of poverty in the last 12–13 years. On semiconductors, he recalled that a company had approached India about 50 years ago to manufacture chips and was turned away, and that when his government announced the Semiconductor Mission, critics again said it was too late: "We went ahead and initiated the mission, and today, India has begun exporting chips," he said. On space, he pointed to the opening of the sector to private players and named Pawan Kumar Chandana, an IIT Kharagpur alumnus and co-founder of Skyroot Aerospace, whose work on India's first privately developed rocket he credited with giving the space programme fresh impetus.

An institute that began in a detention camp

Modi also tied the campus to the freedom struggle, noting that IIT Kharagpur stands on a site that once housed a detention camp for freedom fighters, and that when the institute began, India had only recently gained freedom and had not yet held its first general election. The country then needed engineers for its industries and infrastructure, he said, and the institute's graduates went on to strengthen India's scientific capabilities, including its space and atomic energy programmes. "The journey from aspiration of self-rule to self-reliance is the true driving force behind building a developed India," he said. He closed by asking students and faculty to resolve to reach the 'Viksit Bharat' goal within 20 years: "By 2047, many of you will be in leadership roles... Let us resolve that in the next 20 years, we will achieve the 'Viksit Bharat' goal and work hard to realise it."
